newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - Old problems dog M&R first half.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Old problems dog M&R first half.

text.p: South African industrial holding firm Murray & Roberts Ltd is expected to post a sharp drop in half year profits next week as contract problems continue to dog the firm, analysts said on Friday.
The fall, however, will not come as a surprise for the market as on Monday the group issued its third profit warning in a year.

M&R said it expected its earnings attributable to ordinary shareholders and earnings per share for the six months to end December to be lower than the same period in 1995, despite significant non-operating profits on disposals.
Analysts are expecting headline earnings per share of 23.2 cents to 31.0 from 52.0 last time. They expect the dividend to be held at last time's level of 14.5 cents a share.
But the problems behind the latest cautionary statement from the firm are the same as last year -- contract difficulties and losses from its joint ventures.

"It is essentially the same contracts, additional provisions on the same contracts. The bulk of the business, more than 70 percent, is going relatively well dependent on trading conditions," said Sean Jelley, analyst at SBC Warburg.
The firm has run into trouble with Germany's Siemens over the supply of train carriages to Taiwan's new Dorts rapid transit railway. The carriages failed certain stress tests.
The group is also expected to post losses from its Intershore oil rig joint venture with Dorbyl and British group AMIC Plc.

Analysts said the profit statement was eagerly awaited for details on the extent of the losses and the size of any new provisions. "There are lots of rumours flying about that they may take provisions again," one analyst said.
However, the group's construction operations are seen as performing well in a difficult sector and should post healthy results.
The firm is also set to benefit from its stake in Unitrans which on February 11 posted a rise in half year attributable income to 43.31 million rand from 33.59 million.
Analysts were split on whether this set of results would mark the low point for the firm but some that it would start to post good earnings growth from here.
"We don't really know the extent of the problems. I would think it should be at the bottom, but you never know. I would hesitate to say for sure," said one analyst.

But others said the firm would start to move ahead and sort out its problems this year, paving the way for a healthy 1998. The successive profit warnings have laid waste to the share price which has dipped to 10.40 rand -- a long way from the high of 28.50 rand set in January last year -- and some analysts said the share was starting to look like a bargain.
"With the shares around 10 rand it is an absolute steal," Jelley said.
However, others said the valuation was about fair for the group and it would settle on a price range of 9-10 rand.
Analysts said the firm had taken action, such as replacing staff, on most of its problems, but that the group should have acted sooner and taken all its provisions last year.
"The market has put a question mark over the management. They should have taken a longer-term view," said one.
